analysis.one_liner: Lowers the proof bar for workers claiming age, race, sex, or disability discrimination.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 20, 2025 with support from 8 cosponsors including 3 Republicans, but it has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no markup or vote since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 2009 Supreme Court ruling, a worker claiming age discrimination must prove age was the deciding factor behind an employer's action, not just one reason among several. This bill would flip that back: showing age was a motivating factor would be enough to establish discrimination. If the employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway, the worker can win only a court order or a declaration, not money damages. The same motivating-factor standard would also be written into protections against discrimination based on race, sex, national origin, and disability, and it would apply to claims already pending in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers over 40 who face age discrimination at work, and to a lesser extent workers facing race, sex, national origin, or disability discrimination, who would no longer need to prove the protected trait was the sole deciding factor.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the motivating-factor standard for age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, reversing the Supreme Court's 2009 requirement that age be the but-for cause of an employment decision.

Writes the same motivating-factor standard into Title VII race, color, religion, sex, and national origin protections and into the Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act employment protections.
Defines 'demonstrates' as meeting both burdens of production and persuasion, so a plaintiff who meets the standard has established the violation.
Applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, so workers whose cases are already in court would benefit.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face a lower threshold for losing discrimination suits and more cases surviving early dismissal, though their liability for damages is capped when they prove the same decision would have been made anyway.

drawbacks.text: Even when a worker wins under the motivating-factor standard, the bill denies damages, reinstatement, hiring, or promotion if the employer shows it would have made the same decision anyway, leaving only declarations, injunctions, and fees for that claim — so the practical payoff is often limited.
Applying the new standard to all pending claims is retroactive, which could lengthen or reopen litigation already underway and is the provision employers would most likely contest.

Employers and business groups argue the lower causation standard makes it easier to establish liability with weaker evidence, raising litigation and compliance costs across hiring, firing, and promotion decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For older workers, the bill removes a serious procedural hurdle created by the courts, and the built-in same-decision defense gives employers a real shield that limits damages in mixed-motive cases, which moderates the cost to businesses. The main weakness is practical: in many cases the defense will mean a legal win with little or no money behind it. The cost to employers is genuine but targeted at cases where a protected trait really was a factor in the decision.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it since; it has never come to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on May 20, 2025 with five original cosponsors: Reps. Grothman, Bonamici, Adams, Van Drew, and Fitzpatrick.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
Eight members are now listed as cosponsors — five Democrats and three Republicans — so the bill carries bipartisan sponsorship.
The full action history shows only introduction and committee referral, with no markup, hearing, or floor vote recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers benefit from the bill going nowhere: the easier-to-prove discrimination standard it would create has not become law, and workers over 40 continue to face the harder proof burden the Supreme Court set in 2009.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan in sponsorship — 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans of 8 cosponsors — but all action so far has been introduction and a Republican-held committee's decision not to advance it.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses with 20 or more employees
industries.note: The bill would make it easier for workers to establish age, race, sex, and disability discrimination, increasing litigation risk and the cost of contested employment decisions. The same-decision defense caps damages liability when the employer proves the outcome would have been the same regardless.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress has more than a year left, but the bill's path is narrow: it has 8 cosponsors, no subcommittee or committee action since referral in May 2025, and it would need the Education and Workforce Committee to hold a markup before any floor vote. An identical version of this legislation passed the House in 2020 and died without a Senate vote, and with both chambers closely divided, the most likely outcome is that it again sits without movement unless it is attached to a larger package.
